title: PowerShell Abuse
overview: Investigate a PowerShell script-block observation with an unusual document-application parent.
prerequisites: Be comfortable reading timestamps and windows security or sysmon projection fields.

attack.name: PowerShell
attack.rationale: The behavior in this lesson corresponds to this technique; the fixture models a defensive observation.

hypothesis: An obfuscated PowerShell observation under an office parent warrants process-tree and document review.
evidence: Use event 4104, parent process and script classification, then pivot to process identity and document origin.
false_positive: Internal Office automation can invoke maintenance tooling with similar lineage.
tuning: Verify a specific signed workflow and execution identity before creating a bounded exception.
response: Preserve script-block and process records, scope related executions and isolate if other evidence supports compromise.
prevention: Enable script block logging, AMSI integration and application control. Review Office child-process policy.
validation: Baseline and noisy fixture produce no alerts. The positive fixture produces an alert with linked evidence.
limitations: The fixture uses a preclassified script event with normalized parent context. No script executes.

questions.explanation: 4104 is a PowerShell script-block logging event, whereas 4624 denotes successful logon.

options: The machine had a descriptive name
An office process launched the script interpreter
questions.explanation: Parentage helps distinguish the unusual launch context from ordinary interactive administration.
